articles.title: 'They didn't see it coming' - what does it take to be a traitor?
articles.summary: With the return of the new series of the BBC's Traitors, Minah Shannon opens up about her experience.
articles.body:
When Minah Shannon felt the tap on her shoulder to signify that she had been selected as a traitor in series three of the popular BBC show, she almost struggled to contain her excitement.

"I literally could have done a back flip. I was so excited," she says.

But thankfully the mum, from Liverpool, was able to maintain her composure to make sure she went undetected until the final week.

Hosted by Claudia Winkleman, The Traitors sees contestants split into "faithfuls" and "traitors", with the former looking to find the latter before they are murdered or banished.

The highly-anticipated celebrity version of the show began on Thursday, with stars including Michael Sheen, Jerry Hall, Richard E Grant and Amol Rajan at the round table along with Bella Ramsey, Leigh-Anne Pinnock, Maya Jama and King Kenny.

Minah says she was inspired to apply for the show as she was a "massive fan" of the previous two series.

"I am a massive nerd when it comes to The Traitors.

"I'm just a normal girl from Liverpool going and recording this thing that you love and being a part of a show that you're so obsessed with."

During her time on the show, fans watched as she tricked the faithful contestants by banishing fellow traitors Armani and Linda.

Her performance almost took her all the way to the final, but she was voted out just two days before.

But what does it take to be a traitor and trick the faithfuls into believing she is one of them?

"I'm just a happy, smiley person and they didn't see it coming – that was the fun of it," she said.

"When I became a mum, I just felt like I had this massive responsibility.

"My little girl was just about to turn two.

"It felt like I could be a kid and I was allowed to be a bit naughty, a bit mischievous and just try to get away with murder basically."

Minah says she always had her sights set on becoming a traitor when she applied for the show.

"It's funny because people always say to me 'how does your family trust you' and 'have you always been a good liar'.

"It's not that I'm a liar but I just saw it as a performance like I was acting in a film so my role was to be a traitor and I always wanted to be a traitor.

"I just like the control. I'm a control freak, what can I say?

"I just needed to know who else had that kind of power and I needed to be one of those people so I was so excited."

The Celebrity Traitors series two returned on 1 October at 20:00 BST on iPlayer and BBC One. The series will air two nights a week on Thursday and Friday evenings with a spin-off series Uncloaked airing immediately after.

articles.title: Pope vs Anthropic: Why 'AI consciousness' is dividing Silicon Valley and Vatican
articles.summary: A debate over whether artificial intelligence could have something resembling consciousness has put Anthropic, one of the world's leading AI companies, at
articles.body: A debate over whether artificial intelligence could have something resembling consciousness has put Anthropic, one of the world's leading AI companies, at odds with the Vatican after Pope Leo XIV rejected the idea that machines could replace or surpass human beings.The disagreement surfaced after Anthropic co-founder Christopher Olah reviewed the Pope's first encyclical, "Magnifica Humanitas", ahead of its launch at the Vatican. Olah had accepted an invitation to speak at the event on May 25, but reportedly considered pulling Anthropic out after disagreeing with the Pope's position on AI consciousness.The dispute points to a much bigger question surrounding the rapid development of AI. As companies build increasingly capable systems and deploy them in everyday life, there is still disagreement over whether these systems should be understood simply as tools, autonomous agents or something closer to beings.What did Pope Leo XIV say about AIIn his encyclical, Leo warned against allowing technology to become more important than human beings." ... humanity — in all its grandeur and woundedness — must never be replaced or surpassed"He also wrote, "If technology becomes the ultimate criterion, the human person risks being reduced to data, a cog in a machine or a commodity."The Pope's position clashes with questions Olah has been raising privately about whether advanced AI systems could possess some form of moral status.According to The New York Times, Olah has encouraged religious thinkers to consider the possibility that Anthropic's Claude models could have something resembling moral status.Why is Anthropic thinking about AI's moral statusAnthropic has spent months consulting religious scholars and other experts about how AI systems should behave and what values they should follow. The company has held private discussions with scholars from around the world and required participants to sign nondisclosure agreements, according to the Times.The effort comes as Anthropic pursues rapid expansion, with the company potentially reaching a valuation of $2 trillion.Olah has argued that AI development cannot be separated from questions about values and morality."Those who control AI will impose their own moral vision, which will become the invisible infrastructure of these systems," Olah argued, per the Times.His concerns go beyond philosophical questions. Anthropic has been examining possible real-world risks from AI, including disruption to jobs, cyberattacks and biological threats.AI systems are already being introduced into workplaces, customer services, search, education and other areas where their decisions can affect people's lives.Anthropic's attempt to decide what AI should valueAnthropic says it is trying to address these concerns through outside consultation and a written "constitution" for Claude.The 84-page document is intended to guide how the AI model behaves. The company has also consulted philosophers, religious scholars, psychologists and civil society representatives.Anthropic's in-house philosopher Amanda Askell said she wants the company's models to be "the best of us". Olah, meanwhile, has argued for "some shared notion of goodness that cuts across society in some very broad way," according to the Times.But questions remain over who should ultimately decide what values powerful AI systems should follow. Private discussions between technology companies and outside experts may influence AI behaviour, but they do not amount to public oversight.Olah has also said researchers are encountering behaviour in AI systems that they do not fully understand."I will be honest: We keep finding things that are mysterious, even unsettling. We find structures that mirror results from human neuroscience. We find evidence of introspection. We find internal states that functionally mirror joy, satisfaction, fear, grief, and unease. I don't know what that means, but I think it warrants ongoing discernment," Olah said, according to the Times.At the centre of the dispute is therefore a question that goes beyond the Vatican and Anthropic. As AI becomes more capable and increasingly embedded in society, researchers, technology companies and religious thinkers are still debating what these systems actually are, what rights or moral status they might have, and who should decide the values that guide them.You use AI every day. articles.title: Two Iowa farmers gave up pigs and started growing mushrooms; their abandoned livestock buildings became an artisan food business
articles.summary: Two Iowa farmers have transformed their family's former hog operation into a speciality mushroom business, turning infrastructure once built for thousands
articles.body: Two Iowa farmers have transformed their family's former hog operation into a speciality mushroom business, turning infrastructure once built for thousands of pigs into spaces for growing lion's mane and oyster mushrooms. The Faaborg family, which once raised about 8,000 hogs a year, ended its animal-farming contract in October 2022 after decades in the industry. Their operation, now called 1100 Farm, has repurposed half of a 200-foot hog barn into mushroom-growing and processing space, while a former manure pit has been converted into a freshwater pond. With support from the Transfarmation Project, the family has expanded into value-added products including mushroom tinctures, flavoured salts, coffee and hot chocolate.From pigs to mushrooms: Iowa farmers' big switchThe Faaborg family's move away from pigs followed decades of involvement in Iowa's livestock industry. Rand and Tammy Faaborg began raising pigs as a side business after buying their 25-acre farm. The operation eventually expanded through contract feeding, in which an integrator supplies animals and feed while farmers provide the buildings and labour.The family initially adapted existing structures to hold about 2,000 hogs. Later, they borrowed more than $400,000 to construct two larger hog barns. Rand said it took roughly 12 years to repay the debt.At its peak, the family operation was raising around 8,000 hogs annually. But the economics and demands of the business changed. Rand, who also worked as a welder, described periods when he worked 16-hour days and sometimes 24-hour stretches. He said that over 35 years, his income from his main job increased significantly, while his earnings from raising hogs declined by about two-thirds.Tanner Faaborg pushes for a new directionThe idea of changing the farm's direction gained momentum with the family's next generation. Their son Tanner Faaborg developed an interest in sustainability and climate issues while studying at college.After returning home, Tanner found himself caught between his interest in environmental issues and the realities of the family's hog operation. He began looking for ways to use the existing farm infrastructure without continuing to raise large numbers of animals.The family eventually began working with the Transfarmation Project in 2021, an initiative that helps farmers explore alternatives to intensive animal agriculture. The Faaborgs ended their animal-farming contract on October 23, 2022, according to the project's timeline.The mushroom experiment beginsMushrooms emerged as one possible alternative because they could be grown indoors using existing agricultural buildings. In 2023, the family received a $15,000 research and innovation grant to experiment with mushroom production and develop products.The family reported spending about $35,000 on site preparation, equipment and supplies, as well as branding and website development for the pilot.They began experimenting with speciality varieties, including lion's mane and oyster mushrooms. Instead of buying all their growing material, the family also learned to make its own mushroom blocks using soy hulls and hardwood pellets.The first mushroom crop was harvested and sold in March 2024, according to the Transfarmation Project's timeline.How an old hog barn became a mushroom farmThe family's new business is called 1100 Farm, a name linked to the capacity of the original hog barns.Rather than demolishing the old structures, the Faaborgs began converting them. By 2026, half of one approximately 200-foot-long hog barn had been transformed into a mushroom-growing facility.The renovated space includes specialised fruiting rooms where mushrooms grow under controlled conditions. Other areas are used for preparing growing substrate, developing mushroom spawn and processing the crop.The family has also discussed using the second hog barn for another agricultural venture. One possibility is growing microgreens, although that plan has not yet been implemented.From fresh mushrooms to artisan food productsThe Faaborgs have not limited the business to selling fresh mushrooms. They have developed a range of value-added products designed to give the crop a longer shelf life and create additional revenue streams.1100 Farm currently sells products including lion's mane and reishi tinctures, mushroom salt, lion's mane coffee and lion's mane dark hot chocolate.The family is also working towards expanding its fresh-mushroom sales as production grows. The approach means the former livestock operation is now serving a different type of food market, combining farming with small-scale food processing and direct-to-consumer sales. A 2025 feature in The New York Times significantly boosted 1100 Farm's sales, with the Transfarmation Project reporting nearly 1,000 orders in the days after publication.A manure pit becomes a wildlife pondThe transformation has extended beyond the buildings. A former manure pit that once stored roughly one million gallons of liquid hog manure has been remediated and converted into a freshwater pond.Funding from the US Department of Agriculture's Natural Resources Conservation Service helped support the work.The family says the pond has attracted frogs, ducks and other wildlife. They have also planted native grasses and wildflowers and added trees and shrubs around parts of the property.The change illustrates how the family has repurposed not only its buildings but also other infrastructure associated with the former livestock operation.The money behind the transitionThe Faaborgs' transition has involved several different sources of funding and financial commitments.The family received the $15,000 mushroom research grant in 2023 and reported spending around $35,000 on the pilot. Separately, Transfarmation has a $216,000 four-year contract with the family to document the transition, including costs, labour hours and product margins.The $216,000 is not the reported valuation or annual revenue of 1100 Farm. The family has not publicly disclosed a current business valuation or annual revenue figure.The original hog operation also involved significant borrowing. The family borrowed more than $400,000 to build its two larger hog barns, with Rand saying it took about 12 years to pay that debt.1100 Farm becomes a demonstration hubThe Faaborg farm has since taken on a role beyond its own business. In July 2026, it became the Transfarmation Project's second demonstration hub.The site is intended to show farmers how existing livestock infrastructure can be adapted for other forms of agriculture. It also provides an opportunity to gather information about the practical costs and challenges involved in changing a farm's business model. The family is continuing to develop the mushroom operation while considering additional uses for the remaining livestock infrastructure.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.summary: NEW YORK: The woman who accused members of a Cornell University fraternity of gang rape was “failed” by people obligated to protect her, including campus
articles.body: NEW YORK: The woman who accused members of a Cornell University fraternity of gang rape was “failed” by people obligated to protect her, including campus police and county prosecutor, New York governor Kathy Hochul said Friday.Hochul said at a news conference that she decided to appoint attorney general Letitia James as a special prosecutor to take over the investigation after learning “troubling details” about how authorities have handled the woman’s claims thus far, including that the district attorney closed the case without having anyone interview the accuser or anyone else involved in the alleged attack.“In what world does the district attorney not even interview her, or anyone else involved, or even request the full transcript?” Hochul said. “This woman had already endured something that is utterly unspeakable. And then at every turn, she was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her.”The probe was closed without charges in 2024, but Van Houten reopened it on Monday after the woman sued seven former Chi Phi fraternity members, Cornell and others. The lawsuit alleges she was plied with drugs and alcohol, then subjected to sexual acts by several men while partially or entirely incapacitated. Lawyers for two defendants denied they participated in a sexual assault.Van Houten, who was removed from the case, backed James’ appointment but said the university had not provided the full picture. articles.title: Beth Feeback paid $9.99 for a North Carolina thrift-store painting she wanted to cover with cats; it proved to be an Ilya Bolotowsky work and sold at Sotheby's for $34,375, including fees
articles.summary: A North Carolina artist once walked into a Goodwill store looking for inexpensive material for her own artwork and walked out with what would turn out to
articles.body: A North Carolina artist once walked into a Goodwill store looking for inexpensive material for her own artwork and walked out with what would turn out to be a valuable piece of American abstraction. Beth Feeback paid just $9.99 for a large painting in 2012, not because she admired the artwork, but because she wanted to reuse its canvas for one of her own paintings featuring cats. Months later, a friend's suggestion to check the markings on the back changed the fate of the seemingly ordinary thrift-store find, according to a report by ABC News.The painting turned out to be “Vertical Diamond” by Ilya Bolotowsky, a Russian-born American abstract artist whose work is held by major museums. It was subsequently authenticated and offered at Sotheby's in New York, where it sold for about $27,000 at auction. With the buyer's premium included, Sotheby's listed the final price as $34,375.The extraordinary discovery began with a purchase that Feeback had no reason to regard as an art investment. According to ABC News, Feeback, who lived in Concord, North Carolina, bought the painting in April 2012. She was not particularly drawn to its abstract style. Instead, she saw the large canvas as useful material for her own work. Her speciality was painting cat portraits, and she intended to paint over the existing artwork and create something of her own. The painting reportedly sat on the floor of her art studio for several months.Then a friend urged Feeback to inspect the labels and markings on the back before putting a brush to the canvas.That small piece of advice proved crucial. Feeback discovered the name Ilya Bolotowsky associated with the work and began researching the artist. The painting was identified as “Vertical Diamond,” a geometric abstract work. Rather than covering it with cat portraits, she decided to have it examined and pursue a sale.Contemporary reports said Sotheby's estimated that the painting could sell for between $15,000 and $20,000. That estimate was already dramatically higher than the $9.99 Feeback had paid, but the final result went beyond it. When the painting went under the hammer in September 2012, Feeback watched the auction remotely with family and friends. She had concerns that it might not sell at all, particularly because some other works at the auction were selling below estimates or failing to find buyers. Instead, the Bolotowsky painting attracted a successful bid of roughly $27,000.Sotheby's reported the total sale price as $34,375, a figure that included the premium paid by the buyer on top of the hammer price. ABC News specifically clarified the distinction, making the $34,375 figure different from the amount Feeback actually received from the sale.For Feeback, the result transformed a $9.99 purchase into a significant financial windfall. She told ABC News that she and her husband planned to use the money for long-delayed improvements to their home and to pay down debts. She also joked about the unlikely journey of the artwork: instead of painting cats over Bolotowsky's work, she planned to create her own versions inspired by “Vertical Diamond,” this time incorporating large cat heads.The artist behind the thrift-store discovery had a significant place in the history of American abstraction. Ilya Bolotowsky was born in St Petersburg, Russia, in 1907 and died in New York in 1981. The Smithsonian's Archives of American Art describes him as a Russian-American abstract painter. He immigrated to the United States in 1923 and studied at the National Academy of Design. Bolotowsky became closely associated with geometric abstraction and was a founding member of the American Abstract Artists, an organisation formed to promote abstract art in the United States. His work was strongly influenced by Dutch artist Piet Mondrian and the principles of geometric abstraction. Smithsonian American Art MuseumHis career also included work under the federal art programmes of the 1930s and teaching positions at institutions including Black Mountain College, the University of Wyoming and Brooklyn College. The Smithsonian records his involvement with the Public Works of Art Project and the Works Progress Administration's Federal Art Project.Bolotowsky's work later received institutional recognition, including a 1974 retrospective at New York's Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, according to museum and gallery records. “Vertical Diamond” itself is recorded as a 1966 oil-on-canvas work. Art-market records identify its September 21, 2012 sale and its $34,375 result, consistent with the contemporary reports of Feeback's discovery.The provenance of the painting also helped explain why such a significant work could eventually end up in a thrift store. Reports noted a Weatherspoon Art Museum sticker on the back, connecting the canvas to the University of North Carolina at Greensboro's museum. Contemporary accounts said museum records indicated that Burlington Industries had loaned the painting to the Weatherspoon for an exhibition in 1979. For Feeback, however, none of that history was apparent when she first saw the painting.At Goodwill, it was simply a large canvas she could buy for less than $10. Had her friend's warning come too late, the artwork might have been painted over and its identity lost. Instead, a quick check of the label led to an artist, a title, an auction and a final reported price of $34,375 including the buyer's premium.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Brazil: An election of choice?
articles.summary: On the eve of a bitter election, two Brazilians explain how a country that cheers for politicians like soccer clubs ends up voting not for the candidate
articles.body: On the eve of a bitter election, two Brazilians explain how a country that cheers for politicians like soccer clubs ends up voting not for the candidate it likes more, but against the one it dislikes most — and why, either way, less will change than anyone expects.There is a particular fatigue that settles over a country asked the same question too many times. On Sunday, October 4th, Brazil will be asked it again: Lula or Bolsonaro?This time, the Bolsonaro on the ballot is the son. Senator Flávio Bolsonaro is running in place of his father, Jair, who was convicted last year of plotting a coup and is barred from the race. The Lula is Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva himself: eighty years old, seeking a fourth term, and, across a single career, a union firebrand, the most popular president in modern Brazilian memory, a prisoner whose convictions were later annulled, and a president once more.From India, the contest can look like a referendum on democracy itself. The two countries rhyme in ways that are easy to recite and hard to ignore: continental scale, vast informal economies, loud and partisan media, infrastructure that lags ambition. But from inside Brazil, the election looks less like a battle for the republic's soul than a careful negotiation over which disappointment to live with.Days before the vote, I sat down with two Brazilians — Lucas Bento, a business lawyer, and his compatriot Joaquim Alves — to ask what their country is really arguing about. Neither offered a fan's account. "Neither side has a clean past and beautiful morals," Bento told me. "It's a dispute of narratives: who is right and who is wrong."A free press, in team colorsBento begins by correcting a premise. Brazil's problem, he says, is not a lack of press freedom. "We have a very strong free press," he said. "The government doesn't pressure the channels to take its opinion. But if a channel supports the government, it supports it through and through. If it's against, it's against from the beginning of the candidacy to the end of the term."For decades, that partisanship mattered less, because one network mattered most. TV Globo, Bento recalls, once held more than eighty per cent of the national audience. "When it's eighty per cent of the audience, the opinion of that channel is pretty much the opinion of the country." Globo cultivated an air of impartiality, but Bento's critique is subtler than bias. "Every single decision brings a traffic of ideology," he said. "The fact that you showed it makes it popular. The fact that you decided not to show it — no one would know it."Smaller broadcasters built their audiences on exactly the commentary Globo avoided. Bandeirantes, controlled by the Lebanese-Brazilian Saad family, made stars of anchors who delivered the news and then their verdict on it. RecordTV, owned by Edir Macedo, the founder of the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God, wears its religious convictions in its coverage. By Bento's reckoning, Globo and Band now lean toward Lula; Record and SBT toward the Bolsonaros.The decisive shift, he argues, came when the gatekeeper lost the gate. "Bolsonaro in 2018 was only able to be elected because of the internet," he said. Globo was not with him; neither were the country's intellectual elites. What carried him were what Bento calls "the minority opinions" — not minority populations, he is careful to add, but the views the mainstream had declined to air.This year, the asymmetry is gone. "It's the first time that I see Lula's side being a master of the internet as well," he said. Television, in his view, has become something close to a bystander. "The dispute of narratives on WhatsApp, on Instagram, on TikTok — that's what is making the difference."The soccer-club theory of politicsI put to them the question that, from abroad, seems unavoidable. How does a nation this proud keep in contention a family whose patriarch was convicted over a coup plot — one that, prosecutors said, contemplated assassinating Lula — and whose supporters ransacked the seats of government in Brasília while he sat out the aftermath in Florida?Bento's answer was about information, not ideology. For most of modern Brazilian history, he explained, the millions of Brazilians with little formal education got their news almost entirely from television; the morning paper belonged to a narrower, better-schooled slice of the country. Then cheap smartphones arrived. "Every single person would be bombarded with information the whole day, from various different sources," he said. "They were not well prepared to receive this amount of information. They cannot really tell what's right and what's wrong — especially now, with artificial intelligence, when you can see photos and videos that are fake."The result, in his account, is not that voters forgive the scandals. It is that they disbelieve them. "Why do we even consider candidates with criminal records?" he asked. "Because the population doesn't see the backgrounds as weird. They don't even believe the backgrounds."Alves sees the same reflex on both sides. Bolsonaro's base follows him blindly and reads every charge as persecution, he said; Lula's base does exactly the same. To each camp, its own man's time behind bars proves nothing. "That's not true," he said, ventriloquizing the partisan. "It was planted."Bento then offered the image that, more than any poll, explains the mood. "We like to support our soccer teams, right? Doesn't matter if it's a good season or a bad season, we always support our team. Now people do it with politicians."A ban, nine days outIf this campaign has a defining controversy, both men agreed, it is neither the Amazon nor inflation. It is the "bets."Online betting exploded in Brazil over the past several years, first through offshore sites and then through a licensed domestic market. Betting companies are now, in Bento's words, the biggest sponsors of the country's soccer clubs and of its most famous influencers. They have also become, critics argue, a public-health crisis concentrated among the poor. "People were getting the money to eat and putting it on bets," Bento said. "Losing this money, and not being able to eat. Bringing hunger back."On September 25th, nine days before the first round, Lula signed an executive order banning online betting outright. It took immediate effect, though Congress must approve it within a hundred and twenty days. Flávio Bolsonaro called it an "electoral measure"Here the lawyer in Bento takes over. The irony, he notes, is that Lula's own government built the legal market — regulation arrived only about two years ago, Alves pointed out and charged each licensed operator a concession fee of thirty million reais, roughly five to six million dollars. It also created a national self-exclusion registry, which Bento calls the "auto-ban," letting a gambler block himself from every licensed site at once. "But addiction is a psychiatric issue," Bento said. "If the person could say no, there wouldn't be an addiction."He does not presume to say whether betting should be banned — "I'm a doctor of law, not a medical doctor" — but the timing offends him professionally. "You paid me five million dollars, I gave you the concession, and now I ban the concession and don't give you back the money," he said. His verdict: "Incoherent, but convenient."The ban splits the country along unexpected lines: soccer culture and the influencer economy against, the intellectual class and families who have watched a relative lose everything to an app in favor. If the polling holds, the second camp is the larger; recent surveys, Reuters reported, show roughly three-quarters of Brazilians support a complete ban. Bento sets the move beside another pre-election gift, discounts of up to eighty per cent for a decade's worth of graduates settling their federal student loans. "He used the machine very well," he said — the machine being the apparatus of incumbency.Hanging over all of it is the judiciary. Bento ranks the collapse of Banco Master as the biggest banking scandal in history, and alleges that it reaches as many as two-thirds of the Supreme Court — a sweeping charge, and his own. He also cites a recent ruling in which, he says, the Court overturned an order to take down a false report about Flávio Bolsonaro, on free-speech grounds. "False information," he said, "is never freedom of speech."Eggs, orange juice, and sovereigntyThe other force in the race comes from abroad. President Trump, Bento says, backs Flávio Bolsonaro and is openly hostile to Lula; at the last G7, he said. The two presidents could barely bring themselves to speak, trading jabs through their speeches instead.Flávio's pitch, as Bento describes it, is a patriotism routed through Washington: love of Brazil, expressed as alignment with the United States. Lula's is the reverse, and Bento tells a story to show it. At a summit in 2003, Lula's first as president, the leaders rose to applaud as George W. Bush was announced. Lula stayed seated and, by Bento's account, pulled his standing foreign minister back into his chair. Asked why, Lula is said to have replied that no one had stood when he walked in. "Brazil is a country with sovereignty and independence, just as the U.S.," is how Bento renders the logic. "If someone stands in applause when I arrive, I stand in applause. If someone doesn't, I don't."When Trump raised tariffs on Brazilian goods last year, Lula's response, per Bento, was a shrug: if America didn't want Brazil's products, he would sell them elsewhere. In Bento's telling, the standoff ended at the American breakfast table. "In two days, there were no eggs, no orange juice," he said, and Washington backed down. The real sequence was slower and messier — relief on many Brazilian food imports came months later — but the parable is the point. Sovereignty is a campaign issue in Brazil now, and Lula has planted his flag on it."We don't need to put on the Brazilian T-shirt and say we are proud," Bento said, summarizing Lula's posture. "We are proud because we respect ourselves." It is a pointed line in a country where the yellow national-team jersey became the uniform of Bolsonaro's movement.The lesser dislikeWho wins? Both men expect no candidate to clear fifty per cent on Sunday, forcing a runoff on October 25th that will go, as Bento put it, "until the last moment." He forecasts Lula — not out of affection but out of the arithmetic of aversion. "There are a lot of people who won't vote for Lula in the first round," he said. "But when it comes to a decision between Bolsonaro and Lula, it will be a decision on which one I oppose more. And there are more opposers of Bolsonaro than opposers of Lula."Alves put it more plainly. "It's not the one I like the most," he said. "It's the one I like less — the one I'm not able to vote for." Bento, who declined to reveal his own ballot, said he would decide the same way, and so would most of the country. "Some people cannot stand looking at Lula because of their ideological issues," he said, "and some people cannot stand looking at Bolsonaro because of their psychological issues." It is hard to miss which half of that sentence carries the sharper edge.And once the votes are counted, what changes? "Way less than we think," Bento said. "It doesn't matter who wins," Alves added. Bento pointed to Jair Bolsonaro's own term, Brazil's first openly right-wing government since the military dictatorship, an arrival that was supposed to be seismic. It changed little, he said. A powerful Congress and a strong judiciary, bruised as it now is, absorb the shock of any single president. "We will move forward with more of the same," he said. "Fortunate or unfortunate."It is tempting, from abroad, to read this election as a battle for a democracy's soul. The Brazilians I spoke with described something more durable and more sobering: institutions strong enough that no single president can remake the country, and an information ecosystem chaotic enough that no single fact can settle an argument. Indian readers will recognize much of it — the WhatsApp forward, the anchor as partisan, the giveaway timed to the ballot. On Sunday, Brazilians will cheer for their teams. On Monday, the country will still be there, largely as it was. Whether that is Brazil's weakness or its quiet strength depends, like everything else this season, on which team you support.Quotations have been condensed and lightly edited for clarity.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1975, lawyer John Swenson ordered rocambole garlic out of curiosity; decades later, his collection helped spark America's Garlic Revolution
articles.summary: In 1975, while practising as a lawyer, John Swenson became interested in alliums while flipping through a seed catalogue.
articles.body: In 1975, while practising as a lawyer, John Swenson became interested in alliums while flipping through a seed catalogue. Out of sheer curiosity, he ordered rocambole garlic bulbs and never looked back. According to Seed Savers Exchange, he became a lifetime member in 1985, listed 133 varieties in its Yearbook over 33 years and donated 150 varieties to its seed bank collection. In 1989, he joined a USDA team on a mission through Russia and Central Asia, which returned with 120 varieties of garlic. His sharing of some of those varieties helped spark a "Garlic Revolution" in the United States seed trade.How John turned his curiosity into detailed historical researchJohn Swenson graduated magna cum laude from Dartmouth College in 1950 with majors in philosophy and sociology before attending Northwestern University School of Law. The organisation describes his successful career in law as one that "translated seamlessly into every aspect of his life". It also credits him with a relentless pursuit of truth and accuracy and a wide-ranging intellect.In the late 1980s, John turned those qualities and his passion for alliums towards a multi-year project on the etymology of the term Chicago. He had come to realise that the common story, that the city was named after a common prairie onion, might be false. The organisation says he researched regional history methodically, teaching himself to read 11 Native American languages along the way.How John’s rocambole garlic discovery led to decades of seed savingJohn's interest in alliums began in 1975 while he was flipping through a seed catalogue. He ordered rocambole garlic bulbs "out of sheer curiosity". The organisation notes that later that same year he first read about Seed Savers Exchange, then called True Seed Exchange, in Organic Gardening magazine.John officially became a listed member in 1984 and a lifetime member in 1985. Over 33 years, it records, he listed 133 varieties in the Yearbook and donated 150 varieties to the organisation's seed bank collection. He also acted as an advisor to Seed Savers Exchange for several years. The organisation adds that John mentioned he often ate 12 varieties of garlic in a day.How a 1989 USDA mission brought 120 garlic varieties backJohn joined a USDA team of biologists in 1989 on a collections mission through Russia and Central Asia. The team searched remote hillsides and bustling marketplaces for every garlic, onion, shallot and carrot possible. Although the team entered what was then the USSR fully accredited, foreign agencies often treated its members with suspicion.Seed Savers Exchange states that John, who stood 6'2", remembered being assigned the smallest seat on a flight from Moscow to Ashgabat. He recalled that the only flights available to Americans were at night. "It was like a military drill," he said, laughing. "They didn't want us American spies to fly out during the daytime because we could see." The organisation reports that the team returned with 120 varieties of garlic alone.How John Swenson helped spark America’s Garlic RevolutionUSDA materials are generally kept in their collection, but John procured samples from as many of the USSR accessions as possible and grew them all in his backyard. He later shared his entire collection with Seed Savers Exchange, which became the foundation of the organisation's garlic collection. He also listed many of his garlic varieties in the Exchange and later sold much of his collection to Filaree Farms in Washington. Of his approach, John said: "My attitude is, what good is knowledge if you can't share it?"His efforts to share helped spark a "Garlic Revolution". The number of garlic varieties available in the United States seed trade rose from 18 in 1987 to 274 by 2004. In 1991, it adds, John wrote "Chicagoua/Chicago: The Origin, Meaning, and Etymology of a Place Name" for Illinois Historic Journal, after finding the diary of Henri Joutel, a French soldier who travelled through the area in 1687. Even in retirement, John continued to help people track down varieties and volunteered with the Chicago Botanic Garden. "I have an ongoing project of selecting and donating unusual seeds," he explained. John Swenson passed away peacefully in his sleep on 9 July 2024, aged 95.You use AI every day. articles.title: Delhi Police registers 3 FIRs over protests demanding CEC Gyanesh Kumar's resignation
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Delhi Police on Saturday registered three FIRs in connection with Friday’s protests by student organisations, political parties and civil
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Delhi Police on Saturday registered three FIRs in connection with Friday’s protests by student organisations, political parties and civil society activists who attempted to gather at Jantar Mantar demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.Two FIRs were registered at Parliament Street police station and one at Connaught Place police station, a senior police officer said. The cases invoke Section 223 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), which deals with alleged disobedience of an order duly promulgated by a public servant.No individual or organisation has been named as an accused in the FIRs, the officer said. However, details of organisers and organisations that proposed or participated in the demonstrations have been included in the contents of the cases.The FIRs follow a day of protests across central Delhi, where thousands of opposition activists, students and youth organisation members attempted to march towards Jantar Mantar. Police detained around 1,000 protesters as they tried to cross barricades and reach the designated protest site.The demonstrations involved the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), All India Students' Association (AISA), Students' Federation of India (SFI), National Students' Union of India (NSUI), Indian Youth Congress (IYC) and other organisations. Protesters were demanding Kumar’s resignation over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and alleged mass deletion of voters.Police had repeatedly announced that gatherings were not permitted at Jantar Mantar. Protesters were stopped at several locations, including Firoz Shah Road and Ashoka Road, with some attempting to push past barricades. AISA president Neha Bora and several other activists were among those stopped.AAP leaders Saurabh Bharadwaj, Atishi and Sanjeev Jha were detained, while Rajya Sabha MP Sanjay Singh was stopped while heading towards the protest. NSUI president Vinod Jakhar and activists from SFI and other student groups were also detained.Security was stepped up across central Delhi, with around 5,000 Delhi Police and paramilitary personnel deployed. Entry and exit gates at 12 metro stations were closed and internet services were suspended in parts of central Delhi amid the protests.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: To reclaim its sovereignty, Senegal must approach debt differently
articles.summary: The country must break the cycle of flawed structural adjustment that only feeds its debt crisis
articles.body:
Earlier this month, the International Monetary Fund and Senegal announced a new loan programme worth $2.2bn. This came after a previous deal was suspended following the discovery in July 2024 of concealed debt equivalent to approximately 25 percent of the country’s GDP, which brought public debt to over 130 percent of GDP, one of the highest ratios in Africa.

This is what might be called a democratic betrayal of debt: The Senegalese people, who had been assured that their country was a model of macroeconomic stability, were presented with a bill that had been accumulating in secret for years.

The discovery caused outrage and much public debate about how Senegal has been managing its debt. The idea of economic independence gained momentum and helped the governing Pastef party secure 80 percent of seats in the parliamentary elections in November that year.

Today, almost two years later, the sovereignty agenda that animated the Senegalese voters is in jeopardy, not through formal renunciation, but through a gradual shift of framework, vocabulary and objective. The government is treating the international financial institutions as the only viable recourse for managing foreign debt instead of seeking a less painful alternative approach.

Senegal has been one of the IMF’s most continuous programme countries. It has repeatedly sought its assistance since 1979.

The structural adjustment introduced by the fund and the World Bank produced stagnation, rising poverty and no economic transformation. It systematically dismantled the institutional infrastructure through which economic change could have been achieved.

In 2004, the country was approved for debt relief under the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries Initiative (HIPC) and got $488m of its debt cancelled, but had to accept adjustment conditionalities, including privatisation of state companies and deregulation, which impacted access to essential services, decent employment, small businesses, and the poor. The relief was real; the structural transformation it was supposed to enable remained elusive.

The question today is who failed whom first. Recalculations put Senegal’s real public debt at the end of 2023 at 99 percent of GDP, compared to the 74 percent initially reported. A divergence of 25 percentage points of GDP, maintained over several consecutive years, is not an accidental omission. The IMF attributed the error to the Senegalese government

This was, at minimum, a systemic failure in the exercise of a conventional responsibility. The institution’s aim, on this reading, is not the development of debtor countries, but their maintenance in a disciplined poverty.

The continental record confirms Senegal is no exception. African countries in IMF programmes have struggled with debt management. Zambia started borrowing from the IMF in the 1980s. The conditions the fund imposed – trade liberalisation, public spending cuts and privatisation – caused its economy to shrink.

Zambia was then forced to seek HIPC relief as well. It was approved but implementation was repeatedly delayed over the painful adjustment policies requested.

Ethiopia also faced delays of several years after it requested debt treatment in February 2021 under the G20 Common Framework. It was not until March 2025 that terms were agreed with creditors – more than a year after it defaulted on debt. Meanwhile, austerity measures imposed as part of a $3.4bn agreement with the IMF led to rising poverty and inequality.

The position advanced here is not a wholesale rejection of external financing, but a call for a different sequence: debt treatment rather than restructuring; audit and accountability before new conditionality; fiscal space for productive investment rather than catch-up taxation; ownership and control over natural resources, rather than ceding them to foreign powers; sustaining social protection rather than curtailing essential services; and the grounding of any borrowing negotiation in a regional and continental balance of power rather than in a structurally unequal bilateral exchange.

Concretely, the Senegalese parliament, jointly with civil society, must without delay create the institutional conditions for a citizens’ debt audit, structured around three democratic minimums: was the debt legal, was it legitimate, did it serve the people?

This should lead to an independent examination of all debt contracted between 2019 and 2024, including the responsibility of arrangers, creditors and the IMF’s own surveillance failure, as a prerequisite for any new debt conditionality, alongside a suspension clause on the service of disputed debt for the duration of the audit.

On fiscal policy, the country needs a differentiated approach. When seeking to expand its tax-to-GDP ratio, it should not raise taxes across the board and cut social spending. Instead, it should focus on taxing extractive industries and wealthy individuals.

A minimum share of state investment in infrastructure, agro-industrial transformation and energy should be protected. The terms of derivative instruments linked to domestic debt, notably the Total Return Swaps, should be capped and made public.

When seeking debt restructuring under the G20 Common Framework , it should aim for a binding timetable and a less asymmetric arbitration mechanism. Any new conditionality accepted should carry a reversibility clause, triggered by pre-defined thresholds, in the event of a major economic shock, to avoid self-defeating austerity.

Hydrocarbon revenue should have its own safeguards, resting on four pillars: a transparent stabilisation fund that accumulates revenue surpluses during boom periods; a dedicated investment envelope for productive and social sectors, including energy transition, agricultural transformation, education, health, water, sanitation and digital infrastructure; an active liability management strategy prioritising the reduction of the costliest components of the external debt; and robust citizen participation and parliamentary oversight over hydrocarbon revenue allocation.

Finally, Senegal should enshrine in national legislation the requirement of prior parliamentary authorisation and full disclosure of any public borrowing.

Senegal cannot do all of this alone. It needs to build a South-South coalition with other African countries struggling with debt to collectively weigh on debt restructuring terms. This is precisely the argument Burkinabe President Thomas Sankara made to the Organisation of African Unity in July 1987: creditors coordinate, borrowers should too.

The Borrowers’ Platform, established in April, is the first institutional answer to that call. It must fulfil three functions: close the information and capacity asymmetry between creditors and debtors; develop common positions on conditionality provisions incompatible with developmental sovereignty; and give collective expression to the principle affirmed in UN General Assembly Resolution 1803 of 1962, that peoples retain inalienable authority over their natural wealth.

In coordination with the African Union, Senegal can help set up a framework enabling African governments to demand a binding 20-to-30-year moratorium on debt service, resting on four provisions: the immediate suspension of all payments without accumulation of arrears; the mandatory allocation of freed resources to sovereign development expenditures, according to priorities set by national parliaments rather than creditors; a multilateral legal framework under UN auspices, shielding the mechanism from the regressive conditionalities of the Paris Club and the IMF; and a mid-term review clause based on human development indicators.

Senegal should also champion a regional mutualisation of liquidity risk on sovereign issues within the West Africa Economic and Monetary Union (WAEMU). The country should also set up a strategic and sovereign process to establish its own currency in collaboration with other countries that currently use the West African CFA franc. The government needs to understand that borrowing in foreign currencies is skyrocketing its debt payments.

In all of these efforts, Senegal’s parliament should play a key role. As the institution which was given a broad mandate in the 2024 elections, it needs to lead the way on establishing a new approach to foreign debt anchored in transparency, legality and sovereignty.

The alternative – accepting the restructuring on current terms and deferring the sovereignty agenda to a later phase – would not be pragmatism. It would be replication of a model that has failed Africa for 40 years.

The Senegalese people deserve better than a better-managed version of structural adjustment. They voted for a rupture. Parliament must hold to that mandate.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: In 2002, British choirs began singing to raise money for clean water; this year, the project marks its 25th year and has raised nearly £1.4 million
articles.summary: Every September, hundreds of singers gather together by the River Thames to turn music into a public fundraiser for clean water and sanitation.
articles.body: Every September, hundreds of singers gather together by the River Thames to turn music into a public fundraiser for clean water and sanitation. Sing for Water brings together choirs from across the United Kingdom as part of the Totally Thames festival, with participants performing water-inspired choral songs while raising money for WaterAid.In 2026, the riverside choral event marks its 25th year. Up to 500 people from more than 40 choirs from across the country are expected to take part. As per Thames Festival Trust, the event was co-founded in 2002 by Thames Festival Trust and composer, singer and musical director Helen Chadwick. Since then, Sing for Water has raised nearly 1.4 million pounds to help change and save lives around the world.How will Sing for Water bring hundreds of singers together in 2026In 2026, Sing for Water marks 25 years of bringing choirs together beside the River Thames. As part of the Totally Thames festival, the event takes place every September and brings up to 500 singers from more than 40 choirs across the United Kingdom to perform water-inspired songs.This year, the event takes place for the first time in the courtyard behind the OXO Tower, where audiences can be seen dancing and singing along in celebration. The choir will be led by conductors Sharon Durant and Ben See. Each participating choir first rehearses the specially curated music separately before coming together for a collective rehearsal the day before the final performance.The event has raised nearly 1.4 million pounds since 2002Sing for Water was co-founded in 2002 by Thames Festival Trust and renowned composer, singer and musical director Helen Chadwick. Over its history, Sing for Water has raised nearly £1.4 million to change and save lives around the world. The project has also become a way for a different community of people to connect with WaterAid’s mission.Megan Elworthy, Senior Community and Events Fundraising Officer, said the event has been more than a fundraiser and described its impact as reaching far beyond the stage. She said the project brings creativity, compassion and collective joy into WaterAid’s work. Sing for Water remains part of the Thames Festival Trust’s artistic programme.Sing for Water raises money for clean water and sanitationThe fundraising behind Sing for Water supports WaterAid, whose vision is a world where everyone has access to clean water, sanitation and hygiene.The Thames Festival Trust says millions of people around the world are living without access to clean water and sanitation. It describes the crisis as one that costs lives and damages the chances of community development. Each singer taking part raises a minimum of £50.The trust says it costs £15 to give one person access to clean water for the rest of their lives. Based on those figures, the event connects each singer’s fundraising with WaterAid’s work to improve access to clean water.Choirs rehearse separately before joining the final performanceThe event brings together individual choirs before they perform collectively as one larger group. Choirs rehearse separately before joining the full group for a collective rehearsal on the day before the final performance. Their programme is built around specially curated music inspired by water. In 2026, Sharon Durant and Ben See are leading the choir, while Una May Olomolaiye is among the guest conductors.The event is part of Totally Thames, an annual September season of arts and culture taking place on, beneath and along the River Thames. Sing for Water adds a choral performance and fundraising element to that wider programme.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 1945, a British submarine sank Nazi U-864 off Norway; 81 years later, authorities recovered 22 mercury containers from a wreck believed to have carried as much as 67 tons of mercury
articles.summary: In February 1945, the British submarine HMS Venturer sank the German U-boat U-864 off Norway’s Fedje island, killing all 73 people aboard.
articles.body: In February 1945, the British submarine HMS Venturer sank the German U-boat U-864 off Norway’s Fedje island, killing all 73 people aboard. More than eight decades later, the wreck has become the centre of a very different problem: a potentially massive mercury cargo that remains on the seabed. In June 2026, Norwegian authorities recovered 22 mercury containers from the wreck during an underwater investigation, as per a report by Diario AS.According to Norway’s Coastal Administration, Kystverket, a wartime Japanese order found in British archives referred to 1,867 mercury containers intended for U-864. If the entire shipment was loaded, it would have amounted to between 65 and 67 tonnes of metallic mercury. However, there are no surviving loading documents that confirm exactly how much mercury was actually aboard when the submarine sank.The submarine’s final missionU-864 was a German Type IXD2 submarine that was travelling from Germany via Norway towards Japan during the final months of World War II. Its mission, known as Operation Caesar, involved transporting specialists, military equipment and materials intended to support Japan’s wartime industry.Among the cargo was mercury, a strategically important material at the time. The submarine never reached Japan. On February 9, 1945, HMS Venturer located U-864 off the Norwegian coast. The British submarine fired torpedoes while both submarines were submerged, striking U-864 and breaking it apart. Norwegian authorities describe the encounter as a unique event in naval history: the first known instance of one submerged submarine sinking another submerged submarine. All 73 people aboard U-864 died, including two Japanese engineers. The wreck came to rest at approximately 150 metres below the surface, around 4 kilometres west of Fedje. It remained undiscovered for decades.Wreck found nearly 60 years laterU-864 was located by the Norwegian Navy’s vessel KNM Tyr in 2003. Investigations subsequently established that the submarine had broken into two major sections, with additional debris scattered around the site. The potential mercury cargo quickly became the central concern.Norwegian authorities say the Japanese wartime order discovered in British archives called for 1,867 containers. If all had been loaded, the mercury cargo would have weighed approximately 65-67 tonnes. But because the original loading documents have not been found, the figure remains an estimate rather than a confirmed inventory.That distinction is important. The wreck is believed to have carried up to 67 tonnes, rather than authorities having established that precisely 67 tonnes went down with it. What is certain is that mercury remains in and around the wreck.Norwegian government records say an area of approximately 47,000 square metres around U-864 is contaminated with mercury. Analyses and calculations have indicated that about 4 kilograms of mercury per year are leaking from the contaminated area.Why mercury is such a concernMercury is a persistent environmental contaminant. Unlike many substances that degrade naturally, mercury can remain in the environment and move between water, sediments and living organisms. Of particular concern is methylmercury, a form that can be produced by microorganisms under certain environmental conditions. It can accumulate in aquatic organisms and become increasingly concentrated higher up the food chain.That is why mercury contamination around a marine wreck can become an issue extending beyond the immediate site. Norway has monitored fish and shellfish around U-864 for years. Authorities have also imposed precautionary dietary advice relating to seafood caught close to the wreck site. The Norwegian government's historical overview records that such advice was introduced in 2005 for pregnant and breastfeeding women and young children.Robots reach the mercury cargoThe latest chapter began after Norway commissioned a new investigation of U-864. In August 2024, the Norwegian Ministry of Trade, Industry and Fisheries instructed Kystverket to conduct further surveys of the wreck and surrounding seabed. The objective was to reduce uncertainty around the condition of the submarine, its mercury containers, the surrounding sediment and the feasibility of recovering some of the cargo.A seabed survey was carried out in May 2025. Kystverket used remotely operated underwater equipment to examine the wreck and its surroundings, including the keel structures where the mercury containers were believed to be stored. The next stage brought investigators directly to the cargo.In June 2026, workers focused on the bow section and exposed six keel boxes. In two of the forward boxes, they found mercury containers. Twenty-two containers were brought to the surface for examination. Investigators also found free-flowing mercury inside some of the keel boxes and in the seabed around the wreck. Kystverket initially estimated that roughly half a tonne of mercury had been recovered from the keel boxes. The operation also revealed how badly the containers had deteriorated after more than 80 years underwater.About 80% of the recovered containers showed damage and leakage, according to Kystverket. Several were marked “Almaden”, referring to Spain’s historic mercury-producing region and providing clues about the origin of at least part of the cargo.The cleanup itself created a problemRecovering mercury might appear to be the straightforward solution, but the 2026 operation demonstrated why authorities are cautious. Working around the wreck can disturb contaminated sediment and potentially release mercury into the surrounding environment. Kystverket's assessment found that free mercury was present both inside the keel boxes and in the seabed.Its September 2026 report concluded that it is technically possible to reach the mercury containers using remotely operated underwater vehicles. But it also found that work around the wreck could cause mercury and contaminated sediment to spread. This has created a difficult engineering calculation: removing mercury could reduce a long-term pollution source, but the process of reaching damaged containers could temporarily increase contamination.Norway now considers sealing the wreckAfter its 2025-26 investigation, Kystverket assessed two broad options: attempting to recover mercury containers before covering the site, or moving directly to covering the wreck and contaminated seabed.The agency concluded that both approaches could reduce environmental risk over the long term. However, it said recovering the cargo carried greater risk of mercury spreading during the operation and would be significantly more expensive than covering the site. Kystverket therefore recommended that the wreck and contaminated sediments be covered as a permanent environmental measure.The agency said a cover would provide a more predictable solution and lower environmental risk during implementation. It also noted that even if some mercury were successfully removed, the site would still need to be covered afterwards. That recommendation is not yet the final decision. Kystverket submitted its assessment to Norway’s Ministry of Trade, Industry and Fisheries, which will decide what action should be taken.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Yemen’s army claims over 1,500 Houthi casualties in past 24 hours
articles.summary: Government forces close a key crossing connecting Houthi-held al-Houban to government-held Taiz city.
articles.body:
Yemen’s internationally recognised government forces have carried out nearly 500 military operations, killing or wounding 1,540 Houthi rebels in the past 24 hours, according to the army.

Warplanes, drones, artillery, missiles and rocket launchers were used to target Houthi positions in various parts of Yemen, military spokesman Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili said on Friday evening.

Most of the casualties came in the governorate of Taiz where the operations halted the Houthi advance, al-Nazili said. The government-held city of Taiz has become a focal point of the renewed fighting .

The army spokesman did not mention any casualties among government forces.

On Saturday, the army’s media official Ammar al-Sami’i told Al Jazeera that the government had closed the al-Houban crossing in Taiz.

The crossing had previously been closed for nine years and was later reopened to civilians in 2024 for “humanitarian reasons”, Sami’i said, as the road is one of Yemen’s most important connections between territory held by the opposing sides. It connects Houthi-held al-Houban to government-held Taiz city.

Sami’i said security reasons are behind the closure, following an attempt by the Houthis to infiltrate Taiz via the road, attacks in the vicinity and a general military buildup.

A fragile truce struck between the government and the Houthis in 2022 collapsed in July this year, and fighting in Yemen has escalated significantly since then.

In mid-September, the Houthis swept across parts of western Yemen, seizing the port city of Mocha and key strategic islands in the Bab al-Mandeb strait.

Since then, anti-Houthi forces have largely stabilised the front lines.

Hundreds of thousands of people have been displaced since the fighting restarted.

Yemen has been embroiled in civil war since the Houthis seized the capital of Sanaa in 2014, forcing the internationally recognised government to retreat to Aden.

articles.title: Boy, 6, who died in Llanfairfechan crash named as Harrison Jones
articles.summary: Harrison Jones was killed after being struck by a Ford Transit Tipper outside his home in Llanfairfechan.
articles.body:
A six-year-old boy who died when he was struck by a van outside of his home has been named as Harrison Glynne Jones.

In a tribute on a fund-raising page launched to support his family, he was described as a "cheeky chappy, full of character with a personality that could light up a room", and who had been "loved more deeply than words could ever express".

Officers were called to reports of an incident involving a white Ford Transit Tipper and a child on Mill Road in Llanfairfechan, Conwy county, after 17:00 BST on Thursday, where Harrison was pronounced dead at the scene.

North Wales Police said a 39-year-old man had been arrested and later released under investigation.

Teddies and flowers left at scene where six-year-old boy died in crash

The GoFundMe fund-raiser was launched by Kate Jones to help cover Harrison's funeral and memorial costs, as well as household bills and essential expenses while his parents take time away from work to grieve.

By Saturday morning it was nearing its £20,000 target.

"Our family's world was changed forever when Kayleigh and Daryl's beautiful six-year-old son Harrison was tragically hit by a vehicle outside of his own home and sadly passed away at the scene in front of his family," Jones said.

"There are no words that can truly describe the heartbreak and devastation his parents, sisters and our whole family are experiencing," Jones said on the fund-raiser page.

"A child should never be taken from their family so suddenly, under such tragic circumstances and we are all struggling to come to terms with this unimaginable loss," she said.

"Harrison's mum and dad are facing the unimaginable task of saying goodbye to their precious little boy, while trying to somehow navigate life without him so we have set up this fundraiser to help Harrison's parents through the difficult weeks and months ahead."

An investigation into the circumstances of the crash is ongoing and police have asked anyone who witnessed the incident or was in the area around Pen y Bryn Road and Mill Road at the time to get in touch with them.

articles.title: In the 1970s, an Italian priest sold 12,000 piranhas to Europe; 55 years later, his proceeds have funded 350m bridges and an 800m airstrip on a remote Brazilian island
articles.summary: An Italian Jesuit priest once turned one of the Amazon's most feared fish into an unlikely source of income for an isolated community.
articles.body: An Italian Jesuit priest once turned one of the Amazon's most feared fish into an unlikely source of income for an isolated community. Giovanni Gallo organised the preservation and export of about 12,000 piranhas from Brazil's Marajó Island, with the proceeds helping fund bridges, a community dock, a cemetery and an airstrip, according to Brazilian academic research and recent reports by CNN Brasil. His wider work eventually led to the creation of the Museu do Marajó, a museum dedicated to the region's history and culture.The story dates to the 1970s, when Gallo arrived in Marajó, a large island in the Brazilian state of Pará. Brazil's National Institute of Historic and Artistic Heritage, or IPHAN, records that he came to Brazil in 1970 and reached Marajó in 1972. Gallo spent his first years in Brazil in other locations before settling in Marajó.Gallo eventually lived in Vila de Jenipapo, in the municipality of Santa Cruz do Arari. The community was isolated and lacked basic infrastructure. Houses were adapted to seasonal flooding, with residents relying on wooden walkways and elevated structures to move around during periods of high water. A historical account published by Ciência Hoje das Crianças describes the local bridges and walkways as precarious, while academic research records Gallo's efforts to address the community's infrastructure and economic difficulties.The solution he developed was unusual. Piranhas were abundant in the region, but Gallo saw a potential commercial use for the fish. According to a 2016 academic study on the social networks surrounding the Museu do Marajó, he established a laboratory where local women were taught to preserve piranhas. According to CNN Brasil, 12,000 specimens were exported to Europe. The proceeds were used both to pay the women involved and to finance community works.Those works were substantial for a small, flood-prone settlement. The academic research records 350 metres of wooden bridges, a community dock, a cemetery designed for the flood season and an 800-metre runway for aircraft.The piranhas, however, were only one part of Gallo's larger project. As residents began bringing him archaeological fragments found around Marajó, Gallo started collecting them. IPHAN records that the first objects came to him through local residents and that he gradually built a collection in Santa Cruz do Arari in 1972. Brazil's National Museums Registry said the Museu do Marajó began informally in Santa Cruz do Arari in 1972.The museum was formally associated with an organisation called O Nosso Museu de Santa Cruz do Arari, founded on December 16, 1981. In 1983, after conflicts surrounding the museum in Santa Cruz do Arari, the collection was moved to Cachoeira do Arari, where the institution became known as the Museu do Marajó and opened to the public in December 1984.The museum's approach was also unusual for its time. Rather than simply displaying archaeological objects behind glass, Gallo developed interactive exhibits known as “computadores de marca caipira,” or “hillbilly computers.” These handmade wooden structures used panels, strings, handles and mechanical elements to encourage visitors to interact with the exhibits. A 2024 doctoral thesis from the Federal University of Northern Tocantins described the system as a distinctive form of exhibition language built around local knowledge and community participation.Gallo died in Belém on March 7, 2003, aged 75, after spending roughly three decades working in Marajó. Academic and cultural sources describe his activities as extending beyond his religious role into community development, photography, archaeology and museology.You use AI every day. articles.title: An Australian council hired specialists to search two remote cemeteries for lost graves; the project has now located 658 unmarked burials, with 338 at White Cliffs and 320 at Menindee
articles.summary: A long-running search for lost and unmarked graves at two remote Australian cemeteries has identified 658 previously unmarked burials.
articles.body: A long-running search for lost and unmarked graves at two remote Australian cemeteries has identified 658 previously unmarked burials. According to Central Darling Shire Council, which funded and commissioned the project, specialist investigators located 338 unmarked graves at White Cliffs Cemetery and another 320 at Menindee Cemetery. The work was carried out to help identify and preserve graves that had been lost over time, while giving the council a clearer picture of the two historic cemeteries. The findings could also help with future cemetery management and heritage preservation in the region.Specialists searched two remote cemeteriesCentral Darling Shire Council contracted Hunter Geophysics, a company that specialises in locating lost, forgotten and unmarked graves, for the project. The work began in July 2025 and used specialist, non-invasive scanning technology to examine the cemetery grounds without the need for digging. The project focused on White Cliffs and Menindee, two communities within the Central Darling Shire in New South Wales. The area is known for its remote outback setting and long history, with cemeteries containing graves dating back through earlier generations of the communities.Rather than relying only on visible headstones or grave markers, the specialist search was designed to identify burial locations that were no longer clearly marked or recorded. This allowed investigators to map areas where burials were believed to exist even when there was little visible evidence at the surface.658 unmarked graves identifiedThe completed survey identified 338 unmarked graves at White Cliffs Cemetery and 320 at Menindee Cemetery, bringing the total to 658, according to Central Darling Shire Council.The discoveries do not mean that the identities of the people buried at the sites are now known. According to the council, the passage of time means there are no details available about the individuals associated with the newly identified unmarked graves. The scanning project instead established the locations of the burials, helping distinguish them from areas where no grave was detected.The results provide a more complete picture of the cemeteries and give the council information that can be used to protect the burial sites from accidental disturbance.Why locating the graves mattersFinding previously unmarked graves is important not only for cemetery management but also for preserving the history of the communities in which they are located. Central Darling Shire Council said the project would help preserve the history and heritage of its cemeteries and towns. For local authorities, knowing where graves are located can also make future maintenance, planning and development work easier. Areas containing previously unidentified burials can be mapped and managed appropriately, reducing the risk of graves being disturbed during work within the cemetery.The project also adds to broader efforts to document the region's historic burial grounds. Central Darling Shire Council has previously worked on cemetery heritage projects intended to record information about graves and the people connected with the region's history. Council documents describe regional cemeteries as important repositories of historical information about the communities and individuals who lived in the area.A memorial at White CliffsThe newly identified graves are also being incorporated into plans to recognise the cemetery's history. At White Cliffs, a large rock has been placed in the cemetery to provide space for memorial plaques, according to the council's project information.The memorial provides a way to acknowledge people whose burial locations can now be identified even though their names and other personal details have been lost. The use of non-invasive scanning was central to the project. Hunter Geophysics describes its work as using methods that can find and map buried features without excavation, including lost human graves and archaeological remains.Preserving cemetery history for the futureThe discovery of 658 unmarked graves gives Central Darling Shire Council a clearer record of two cemeteries that have accumulated generations of burials. While the project cannot recover the identities of those buried in the unmarked graves, identifying their locations provides an important step towards protecting the sites. The White Cliffs and Menindee survey ultimately turns areas of uncertainty into mapped burial sites. For the council, that information can support future cemetery planning, heritage conservation and respectful management of the grounds, while helping preserve a part of the history of two remote Australian communities.You use AI every day.
