articles.title: US engineers turn dredged river sediment into 3D-printed oyster reefs; six structures are now being tested in Mobile Bay
articles.summary: Every year, engineers dig millions of cubic yards of sediment out of the nation's shipping channels, and most of it has traditionally been treated as
articles.body: Every year, engineers dig millions of cubic yards of sediment out of the nation's shipping channels, and most of it has traditionally been treated as waste to be managed. In Mobile Bay, Alabama, the United States Army Corps of Engineers is testing a very different idea, printing that sediment into dome-shaped reefs to help oysters recover. Six experimental structures were placed in the bay in July 2026 and are now being monitored. If they hold up, the approach could turn navigation maintenance into a source of coastal restoration, and the Corps is finalising a national guide to oyster reef engineering.How the United States Army Corps of Engineers prints oyster reef domesThe idea gained momentum when Mobile District engineers were introduced to the Engineer Research and Development Centre's 3D printing technology. Researchers there collected fine-grained dredged sediment from the Blakeley Island Confined Disposal Facility and developed a specialised, printable mixture. Fox10 reports that the sediment was mixed with clay and printed by large-scale machines into dome-shaped structures. The domes have varied surfaces, openings and internal shapes that give a stable place for oyster larvae to settle. Elizabeth Godsey, who leads regional sediment management and Engineering with Nature work for the Corps, via the Engineer Research and Development Centre website, says the idea came from watching how oysters build reefs that filter and stabilise sediment.Six experimental 3D-printed reef structures in CodenAccording to Digital Visual Information Distribution System, the current test builds on a pilot reef placed at an oyster farm on Mon Louis Beach, Dauphin Island, in October 2025 by the Mobile District and the Mobile Bay National Estuary Program. On 9 July 2026, the Mobile Bay National Estuary Program deployed six experimental structures in Coden. Three are made entirely of dredged sediment, and three are mixed with recycled oyster shell, so researchers can see which attracts more oyster growth. Henry Perkins of the same organisation told Fox10 that the structures will be monitored for six to 18 months to see what life they attract, how they hold up and whether they suit future restoration.How 3D-printed sediment reefs attract oysters and barnaclesStorms, shoreline changes and shifting sediment have contributed to habitat loss and fewer oysters in Mobile Bay. Early deployments are promising. Corps research biologist Al Kennedy says the printed domes are holding up against tides, and that barnacles and oysters settle on them as readily as on terracotta, the ideal reference material. The structures provide hard surfaces where none existed and can act as wave breaks that reduce energy, retain sediment and cut erosion. That matters because oysters are a keystone species in coastal Alabama, improving water quality, sheltering other species and easing shoreline erosion. Kennedy adds that scaling up could also restore capacity at the Blakeley Island facility.What comes next for 3D-printed oyster reefs, a national engineering guide for oyster reefsFuture phases will dig deeper. Kennedy says the team plans to compare durability and oyster colonisation in all-sediment domes against domes of ten per cent oyster shell and ninety per cent sediment. It also wants to use a hopper to print continuously, print on site and on demand to cut transport costs, and find bio-inspired binders for the sediment. Beyond Mobile Bay, the Corps is in the final stages of publishing a national Engineering Practice Guide for Oyster Reefs. For the Corps, the aim is a sustainable cycle in which navigation maintenance directly fuels environmental restoration, redefining what beneficial use of dredged material can mean.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'No formal apology': Buckingham Palace says King Charles will only reflect on slave trade
articles.summary: Buckingham Palace has stated that King Charles will not ‘formally apologise’ for Caribbean slave trade but will not shy away from Britain’s role in the
articles.body: Buckingham Palace has stated that King Charles will not ‘formally apologise’ for Caribbean slave trade but will not shy away from Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade during his upcoming tour.Charles and Queen Camilla will visit the Bahamas and Guyana before travelling to Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM), which will be held from November 1 to 4.The trip comes as Caribbean and African countries push Britain and other former colonial powers to address the legacy of slavery and consider reparations. The issue is expected to feature prominently at the Commonwealth summit.Buckingham Palace said the King’s programme would acknowledge Britain’s colonial past, while keeping the focus on the present and future of the countries he visits.“There are important discussions taking place in various fora about colonial legacy and the intergenerational impact of the transatlantic trade in enslaved persons,” a palace spokesperson said.“The visit programme will therefore not shy away from ‘the darkest days of our past’, as his majesty has described them, but – in keeping with the wishes of our host nations – it will principally be oriented to the vibrant present and promising future of each country.”The Palace also stressed that questions of reparations and official apologies were matters for the British government rather than the monarch.The British government has ruled out paying reparations for slavery.Charles has previously expressed sorrow over the transatlantic slave trade and supported research into the British monarchy’s historical links to slavery.A palace spokesperson said the King had spent years acknowledging the wrongs of the past and working to address inequalities that continue today.“Opportunities will be found during the visit to reflect and renew his personal, wholehearted, and continuing commitment to that process,” the spokesperson said.Caribbean calls for reparations growThe royal tour comes against growing calls from Caribbean and African nations for former colonial powers to compensate countries affected by slavery and its legacy.Between the 15th and 19th centuries, at least 12.5 million Africans were abducted and sold into slavery by European merchants. Britain was responsible for transporting an estimated 3.2 million enslaved people, making it the second-largest European participant after Portugal, according to the report.Charles, as head of the Commonwealth, occupies a particularly sensitive position in the debate. The 56-member organisation is made up largely of former British colonies and represents about 2.7 billion people.Last month, Jamaica formally asked Charles to seek legal advice on whether Britain should pay reparations and said it was encouraged by Buckingham Palace’s engagement with the issue.The Commonwealth’s secretary-general, Shirley Botchwey, said in February that she expected member states to make progress towards beginning negotiations on reparations.The upcoming tour is therefore likely to put Charles’ approach to Britain’s slavery legacy back in focus, even as Buckingham Palace makes clear that the King will not offer a formal apology or commit Britain to reparations.You use AI every day. articles.title: Father left his £600,000 house to one daughter and just £250 to each of two others; the inheritance fight ended in a huge court bill
articles.summary: A father who left his £600,000 home to one daughter, and just £250 each to his other two children, has had his final will set aside by a court.
articles.body: A father who left his £600,000 home to one daughter, and just £250 each to his other two children, has had his final will set aside by a court. Laxmikant Patel died in October 2021, aged 85, and the will had been made two months earlier. His daughter Bhavenetta Stewart-Brown challenged it, and Deputy Master Jason Raeburn called the circumstances of the 2021 document "highly suspicious" before reinstating an earlier will from 2019. Reportedly, Anju Patel, together with her brother, was ordered to pay Ms Stewart-Brown's costs of over £450,000, as well as her own legal fees.Why did the father leave his £600,000 house to one daughterAs reported by the Sun, Anju, 58, claimed her father's decision was down to a growing mistrust of her siblings because "they were only after his property". She also said he complained that Bhavenetta and Piyush had failed to show him "true affection". He was said to have labelled his son a "hugely controlling" figure and to have complained of Bhavenetta's "bad temper" and of her taking "massive advantage" of him. When asked why he had left them anything at all, he reportedly replied: "They have failed in their sense of duty, but as a father I have not forgotten them."Bhavenetta's barrister, Tim Sherwin, described the decision to leave the house solely to Anju as "most odd". He told the judge: "The evidence shows a clear pattern of isolation and control over the deceased on the part of Anju and (her husband) which became especially stark when he was in the hospital at the end of his life-when, of course, the purported 2021 will was made ." Anju's barrister, James Kane, argued that by October 2019 Mr Patel had formed a "sharply negative" view of both Piyush and Bhavenetta. Anju told the court: "I wasn't estranged from my family, I was with my sister. She chose to disconnect from me."What did the 2019 Will say about the £600,000 estateAccording to Cartmell Shepherd Solicitors, ‘Courts do not decide these cases based on whether a Will feels fair. The focus is always on legal validity.’ On the first, the firm says the father "was terminally ill, frail and in hospital subject to Covid restrictions when the Will was made just 2 months before his death". Bhavenetta's barrister urged the judge to rule the 2021 will invalid because it was not properly executed and because Mr Patel, who struggled with the English language, did not "know and approve" its terms.Deputy Master Jason Raeburn upheld a 2019 will and described the circumstances of the 2021 will as "highly suspicious", The Sun reports. On the witnessing of the document, he said: "I am not therefore satisfied that a signature was made by (Laxmikant) in the presence of all the witnesses at the same time, so there was no due execution of the will." The 2019 will had left £50,000 to Anju, with the rest of the estate split into shares of 33 per cent to each of the children and one per cent to a charitable trust. The judge struck out the 2021 will and reinstated the 2019 document, which leaves the three children sharing the estate on roughly equal terms.Cartmell Shepherd says the earlier will, "which divided the estate more equally, was reinstated and Ms Patel (together with her brother) was ordered to pay Ms Stewart-Brown's costs of over £450,000 together with her own legal fees". The Sun reports that Bhavenetta won a six-figure sum after the ruling.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: UK-Iranian dual national arrested over RAF Fairford investigation bailed
articles.summary: The 25-year-old man was arrested in the London borough of Westminster on Thursday.
articles.body:
A UK-Iranian dual national arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts in connection with an incident at RAF Fairford has been released on bail.

The 25-year-old man was arrested in the London borough of Westminster on Thursday. Searches of two properties in the same area have now finished.

A major incident was declared and dozens of homes were evacuated after police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase in Gloucestershire last weekend.

Five other men in their twenties were arrested and were subsequently released on police bail. All five were UK nationals from London.

The investigation into the circumstances surrounding the events are continuing, police said.

Last weekend, the five men aged between 23 and 25 were arrested in the early hours of the morning after vehicles were reported to be travelling towards the base operated by the US Air Force (USAF), sparking a major security incident.

The BBC understands that one of the men had dialled 999 himself, about an hour before a local farmer alerted police to a "large group" of masked men near the vehicles.

They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act, before being released on bail on Monday in what police called an "investigative decision" that was "grounded in experience and strategy".

Prime Minister Andy Burnham chaired a Cobra meeting that afternoon in response. He later said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident, but did not provide any more details.

Tehran has strongly denied any involvement. The Iranian embassy in London said on Monday that it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" what it called "unfounded and malicious speculations" linking Iran to the incident.

RAF Fairford has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.

In recent months, US bombers have taken off from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.

In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".

Late on Monday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told a TV show that it was clear a "foreign actor" had been involved in events over the weekend.

Without providing evidence or giving further details, he told Fox News network's "Hannity" programme: "What happened, what almost happened, what could have happened in the UK over the weekend is a very serious situation. It's one that clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor."

Speaking earlier at the Oval Office, US President Donald Trump said he would not have let the five men arrested out on bail, and that he was "surprised" they had been released.

"We know everything about them, we would not have released them," he said, adding that the UK had worked with the US "very closely" on this.

articles.title: Laura Kuenssberg: Kemi Badenoch has cemented her image. Now she wants to take her party back to its roots
articles.summary: The Conservative leader is expected to set out a return to core conservative principles at the party’s annual conference.
articles.body:
The 2026 Conservative conference is big enough to justify using Birmingham's Symphony Hall as its main stage again.

So, Kemi Badenoch will tread the same stage ageing rockers Marillion took last month - and where sequinned soprano Katherine Jenkins will perform next week. She'll also avoid the humiliation of a national party leader being squashed into a side room at a corporate conference centre (with drapes portioning off the empty space). Simply, the party is able to put bums on seats again - and by that measure, things are looking up.

Badenoch goes into the conference with her own position secure in the party. One senior Tory says "she has actually defied cynics like me" who initially disapproved of her leadership. Her standing with the public has improved and she is now, again on a very simple but crucial measure, much better known. Her allies are sure she has developed a clear identity among the public, confiding: "People now know who she is and they enjoy her interventions - the thing we hear most is I don't always agree with her but I know where she stands."

But Conservative MPs are aware that the party itself still has a much bigger issue - in the words of one shadow cabinet member: "The problem we still have is trust of the party and the brand". The shadow of the years of chaos still looms. And while Badenoch has made good progress since she took the job, most of that was up against an unpopular prime minister, Sir Keir Starmer, on whom she landed plenty of political punches. She has to show "what being Conservative is now", says another senior Tory, taking on a different, more popular, rival in Andy Burnham.

The Tories' warm-up to conference has been so far, so traditional. A proposed dramatic expansion of prison places kicks off Badenoch's second big party get-together. With it, a message that echoes the well-known mantra of the early 1990s Tories, issued by former leader Michael Howard at party conference: "Prison works". They are not just talking about adding on a few cells here and there, but spelling out a monumental increase in the numbers of people that the country locks up.

That follows the announcement of a new "tough love" approach for young people trying to claim benefits. Don't expect the shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whateley, to produce a moment as controversial as when the then-welfare secretary, Peter Lilley, proclaimed from the stage that he had "a little list" of benefit claimants he wanted to root out. But the Conservatives are determined to keep concentrating on the size of the welfare bill – believing it's right to do so for financial and moral reasons.

You can expect to hear more in the week about fundamental conservative principles: people keeping more of their own money, government only stepping in when really required to, pointed concern about the level of the country's debt and public spending. And again, of course, that means Kemi Badenoch disavowing much of what the Conservatives did in office between 2010 and 2024, when the civil service grew, the tax burden grew, a law was passed to try to combat climate change, the list goes on.

She'll set out at some length in the coming days what she sees as classic conservative first principles: the core beliefs the party was founded on and drifted from, she reckons, in the years gone by. If anything, Badenoch told interviewers this week the party was "finally saying what we believe" and "should be more aggressive" in displaying the party's core.

She believes the arrival of Andy Burnham makes that easier. There's a clearer contrast between the two. A senior ally of Badenoch says Burnham has "opened the door to it quite well, as he has harked back to the '70s in a way that I'm astonished by". Suggesting the pleasing atmospherics of Burnham's Labour are just that, atmospherics, the ally adds: "It's like a fairy story where he has come to the rescue of Britain and he has a wand in his hand and nothing else".

As we talked about a couple of weeks ago , the contrasts between Labour and the Conservatives are sharper now Burnham is in post, and the conference season is only serving to exaggerate that. They are both only too happy to emphasise it with their messages, retro or not, designed to show the true souls of their tribes.

But while Badenoch might find it easier to argue clearly with Burnham, rather than tangle with Starmer over process, it is harder to face an opponent who, at least for now, is proving more appealing to the public. And while plenty of Conservatives are hopeful in private that Reform might have peaked, they can't be sure that's true, or that the swathes of voters who abandoned the Tories for Farage's party will return.

Badenoch has always seemed allergic to the idea of doing any kind of deal with Reform, who she dismisses as a party of protest. And her allies hope, and some believe, that Reform's appeal will fade, making the Conservatives again the obvious alternative government. But fundamental arithmetic displays that, for as long as millions of voters on the right are tempted by Farage, it's harder for the Tories to triumph. One shadow minister admits "we've still got a whole battle on the right" even though "Kemi's boldness" is beginning to break through.

So, in the coming next days, prepare for a "classic showing of Tory wares": an attempt by the party's leader to set out their fundamental beliefs about the country and how it should be governed.

There are pockets of nerves that Kemi Badenoch risks rewinding to an previous era. One when another newly confident leader, David Cameron, ushered in the modern Tory party on the conference stage in front of digitally produced green foliage and sunlight. One former cabinet minister warns that it's "the big risk – so easy to slip into an alienating divisive manner – nasty party stuff".

When it comes to policy, and striking the right tone, they warn that Badenoch must "be mindful that she has to win Cheltenham and Maidenhead as well as Clacton".

But Kemi Badenoch is visibly more confident and is aware of the chance in front of her – seemingly unworried about the possible downsides of making an increasingly direct argument to you, eager to stride that mercifully bigger Birmingham stage.

articles.title: Sheffield artists give new meaning to 'slow art' - with tortoises
articles.summary: Tortoises help a Sheffield group get to grips with drawing and painting live subjects.
articles.body:
Budding artists may prefer to focus on a still life as their first subject, rather than a live animal - and one Sheffield teacher is offering the best of both worlds.

Claire Cort, who runs the Ay Up Art class at the White Lion pub in Heeley, had offered dogs for her students to draw, but found the models reluctant to sit still.

Luckily, local reptile owners gave her the perfect compromise, with the beginners honing their skills on tortoises.

Cort said: "It was a crazy idea and people were laughing at me going, 'What? You're going to draw tortoises?' And I'm like, why not?"

Cort, better known as CJ, is a former design, technology and arts teacher who became keen to offer art and craft sessions in her community.

She said: "I started Ay Up Art in 2024 and I started my classes to create affordable events in the area that I live in, which is Heeley."

The 49-year-old said: "I'm not ashamed to say I've suffered from depression for many, many years and I've always found that being creative to me is my happy place, my escapism from a very overthinking mind and it relaxes me."

Cort spent 14 years as a secondary school teacher but said it "took over her life" and the long hours meant she was "neglecting" her dog, Maggie, a Westie, who is now 12-and-a-half years old.

So she gave up teaching to become a dog walker full-time, a job which allows her to spend more time with Maggie and but still follow her passion for art.

Cort felt there was a gap in the market for total beginners and those who doubted they had any artistic talent but wanted to try.

"They may have been told at school, 'you're not good at art'. I want to instil confidence in people.

"I think a lot of beginner artists think you're going to be judged and it's not to do with judging."

Cort believes people should be able to express themselves creatively no matter their age.

"Adults deserve to play and experience the capabilities of their imagination."

Cort had held classes on a variety of themes before landing on the idea of tortoises as a good subject for beginners.

"I tried dog life drawing, which was great but obviously dogs don't sit still for very long. They don't pose for, you know, 30 minutes," she said.

Tortoises, on the other hand, are not known for their speed.

Fortunately for Cort, a friend of a friend, Chris Doar, had two Greek (also known as spur-thighed) tortoises and brought them to the first event in September.

And Charlie and Raspberry proved a hit with the class.

Cort said she was "overwhelmed" by the feedback from those who attended.

"Everybody thoroughly enjoyed it. I had a lot of people texting me, saying how much they enjoyed the event," she said.

"And I've got some attendees who came the last time, they're coming again to the next event. So I haven't got many spaces left on that one."

Cort aims to keep numbers at the classes under a dozen so that she can give each participant individual attention.

Proceeds from Charlie and Raspberry's first appearance went to the family-run South Yorkshire Terrapin and Tortoise Rescue centre.

But Cort said class fees are more usually spent on covering the cost of materials she provides for the budding artists to use.

"What's most important to me is that people leave happy," she said.

"I've had people attend my events that have said, 'I can't draw'.

"That's the whole point of being here. By the end of it, they feel so much more confident with their ability. And that to me is the payment.

"It's not necessarily, you know, the profit I make. It's more to do with how people leave the event feeling happy and more confident."

articles.title: Friends and fitness motivate Jersey Marathon runners
articles.summary: Participants from 19 different countries are taking part in the Jersey Marathon, organisers say.
articles.body:
Runners from around the world are gearing up to take part in the 21st Jersey Marathon.

Organisers said runners as young as six and older than 75 from 19 different countries would be taking part on Sunday.

Road closures or restrictions would be in place from 07:30 to 16:00 BST in St Helier, St Lawrence, St John, St Mary, St Ouen, St Peter and St Brelade, they said.

Runners said they were taking part for a variety of reasons including remembering loved ones, keeping fit and celebrating milestone birthdays.

The main 26.2-mile (42km) race begins at 09:00 BST with a relay event and a marathon mile kicking off shortly afterwards.

More than 2,250 people were expected to take part, said organisers.

Among them is Malcolm Wheatley, who is running as part of a relay team from Faithful Companions of Jesus Primary School.

The team is running to remember a colleague, Theresa Taylor, who died with cancer in February and they hope to raise money for a remembrance garden at the school in her memory.

"We'd like it to be a lovely, peaceful area where the children can sit, pray and reflect, as well as enjoy learning about plants and get involved with gardening," he said.

Jersey resident Charlie Pallot is running the marathon in aid of Cancer Research UK to show support for his mother and grandmother who are both going through treatment.

Pallot, who has raised £7,660, was the top fundraiser at this year's race, organisers said.

He said it was a "very special achievement" but getting fit had also motivated him.

"In my first year of university I had become lazy with my fitness and wanted to get back to feeling and looking good," he said.

Jayne Golborne, from Guernsey, is participating as part of a challenge to complete 10 marathons before her 60th birthday in July next year.

She said Sunday's marathon would be her ninth and the third time she has done the race in Jersey after getting into running in 2018.

"I started with Guernsey Parkrun and got hooked into social running," she said.

"A 5k turns into a 10k, turns into a half marathon and, before you know it, someone's persuaded me to do a full marathon."

Paul Welling, a travel agent from Torquay, Devon, is heading to Jersey as part of a challenge for his 60th birthday last August.

He admitted there were times during the 05:30 training runs which left him questioning his decision.

"But if I'd just thrown myself a party, I wouldn't get to experience 26.2 miles of the beautiful island of Jersey," he said.

"Going into my 60s, I just felt I wanted to test myself and push myself to see what my body was capable of.

"Besides that, birthday cake will taste so much better after burning off 3,000 calories."

Another runner from Devon heading to Jersey is Adam Atkins.

The 43-year-old, who is taking part alongside a friend, said he was raising money for a youth basketball team at the Tiverton Titans and it would not be his last running event of the year.

His said his aim was to "get healthier, lose weight and focus on the good things in life".

articles.title: Manu Ashokan’s Eyes explores the psychology of stalking and women’s safety
articles.summary: What goes on in the mind of a stalker, and how do you stop one before things turn dangerous?
articles.body: What goes on in the mind of a stalker, and how do you stop one before things turn dangerous? That question is at the heart of the upcoming Malayalam web series Eyes, which explores obsession, vulnerability, and control through the perspective of a police officer working on disturbing cases involving women. Directed by Manu Ashokan, the series is set to premiere on October 9.The story follows Tina Sebastian, played by Kani Kusruti, a police officer who investigates disturbing cases involving women. As the investigation progresses, mental health professionals join forces with law enforcement to understand the psychology of stalkers and identify factors that could lead to dangerous situations. The series examines the minds of those involved in stalking while following efforts to protect potential victims.The project marks Manu Ashokan’s third directorial venture, following Uyare and Kaanekkaane. He shared the first glimpse on social media and called the project a special journey. “After Uyare and Kaanekkaane, I’m stepping into my third project as a director, a journey that has been deeply special to me,” he wrote. He added, “A new world. A new story. A new experience. Today, I’m happy to finally share its first glimpse with you,” while announcing that the trailer is out now.Eyes is written by Bobby and Sanjay, based on a story by Anjana Nayar, and produced by T.R. Shamsudheen under Dream Katcher Productions. Its tagline, “Watch, Protect, Defend”, captures its focus on investigation, protection and the psychology behind stalking.Alongside Kani Kusruti, the cast includes Shruti Ramachandran, Nikhila Vimal, Saniya Iyappan and Dev Mohan. Together, they bring to life a story that blends police work with psychological analysis, following characters as they deal with cases that put women’s safety at stake.With its focus on stalking, obsession and the psychology behind such cases, Manu Ashokan’s Eyes brings together police investigation and mental health perspectives in a story centred on the safety and vulnerability of women. The series is set to premiere on October 9.

articles.title: Delhi landfill garbage mountains shrinking, 100 acres reclaimed in 18 months: CM Rekha Gupta
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Delhi chief minister Rekha Gupta on Saturday said the garbage mountains at the city's landfill sites were steadily shrinking as she reviewed
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Delhi chief minister Rekha Gupta on Saturday said the garbage mountains at the city's landfill sites were steadily shrinking as she reviewed waste disposal work at Okhla and laid the foundation stone for new waste processing facilities at Okhla, Ghazipur and Singhola.Gupta said the Delhi government had reclaimed 100 acres of land across the city's three landfill sites over the past one-and-a-half years, with a large portion of the cleared area also being turned green.She said almost all legacy waste at Okhla that existed before January 2025 had been processed."Today, at Okhla, we have processed almost all the legacy waste that was there before January 2025," Gupta said.Government targets legacy and fresh wasteGupta said the government was working on two fronts: clearing the existing garbage mountains while ensuring that fresh waste generated every day did not accumulate into new landfill sites.According to news agency ANI, she said around 3,000-4,000 metric tonnes of fresh waste reaches the sites daily and is being processed round the clock."The garbage currently piled up here is essentially fresh waste generated after January 2025, and that too is being processed round the clock. So, we are fighting on two fronts: one is eliminating waste, and the other is ensuring that the 3,000 to 4,000 metric tons of fresh waste arriving daily is processed immediately, so that new garbage mountains are not formed for future generations," Gupta said.She said the government was working to reduce the existing garbage mountains to zero."People are seeing that the garbage mountains are continuously shrinking and soon a time will come when they will become zero," Gupta said.Gupta also said she had taken what she described as her "last selfie" with the garbage mountain at Okhla."Today I have taken my last selfie with the garbage mountain; after this I have taken a pledge that this garbage mountain will end soon," she said.Taking a jibe at the Opposition, Gupta added, "I had said - garbage mountain, you will have to go; the opposition mocked. Today I will say the garbage mountain is going; now only its back remains."New processing plants at three sitesDuring the programme at the Okhla SLF site, Gupta laid the foundation stone for fresh waste processing plants at Okhla, Ghazipur and Singhola, as well as a biogas facility at Ghazipur. She also inaugurated the M&CW Centre at Kotla Mubarakpur through virtual mode from Okhla.The Okhla plant will be built at a cost of Rs 103 crore and will have a processing capacity of 1,400 metric tonnes per day.The Singhola facility will cost Rs 42 crore and have a capacity of 800 metric tonnes per day, while the Ghazipur plant will have a processing capacity of 700 metric tonnes per day.The facilities are intended to process fresh waste as well as construction and demolition waste. Gupta said the new units would also produce biogas, green energy and manure."Waste should not remain waste; Delhi should use it as wealth," she said, adding that new technologies were being introduced for waste segregation and processing.She said waste and cattle dung would be used to produce biogas and manure as part of efforts to build a technology-driven waste management system.Focus on pollution and waste managementGupta said the government was taking up several measures to address pollution, including work on landfill waste, cleaning the Yamuna, dust mitigation, plantation, road infrastructure and waste management."Our government is tackling pollution from a 360-degree perspective to ensure it gradually decreases. We are working on every aspect, be it addressing the mountains of garbage, cleaning the Yamuna, improving road infrastructure, or managing waste, to ensure the people of Delhi enjoy better air quality. Our resolve and policies are absolutely clear, and we are working 24x7 in the public interest," she said.The chief minister also reviewed the progress of waste disposal work with officials and directed them to accelerate the work according to the stipulated timeline.She said the garbage mountains at Bhalswa, Ghazipur and Okhla had caused inconvenience to people travelling through these areas and said the government was continuing efforts to eliminate them.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
